claim: MreB is an actin homolog that is essential for coordinating the cell wall synthesis required for the rod shape of many bacteria.
source: MreB is an actin homolog that is essential for coordinating the cell wall synthesis required for the rod shape of many bacteria.
evidence: This is stated in the abstract as established background information about MreB's role.

claim: Filaments of MreB bind to the curved membranes of bacteria and translocate in directions determined by principal membrane curvatures to create and reinforce the rod shape.
source: Previously we have shown that filaments of MreB bind to the curved membranes of bacteria and translocate in directions determined by principal membrane curvatures to create and reinforce the rod shape (Hussain et al., 2018).
evidence: This claim is supported by citation to prior work by the authors.

claim: It is both energetically favorable and robust for filaments to bind and orient along directions of largest membrane curvature.
source: We find that it is both energetically favorable and robust for filaments to bind and orient along directions of largest membrane curvature.
evidence: This is a primary finding from the modeling work presented in the manuscript.

claim: Significant localization to different membrane regions results from processive MreB motion in various geometries.
source: Furthermore, significant localization to different membrane regions results from processive MreB motion in various geometries.
evidence: This is a primary finding from the modeling work presented in the manuscript.

claim: The in vivo localization of MreB observed in many different experiments, including those examining negative Gaussian curvature, can arise from translocation dynamics alone.
source: These results demonstrate that the in vivo localization of MreB observed in many different experiments, including those examining negative Gaussian curvature, can arise from translocation dynamics alone.
evidence: This is a primary conclusion from the modeling work presented in the manuscript.

claim: Membrane curvature can both be induced by proteins that bind to membranes as well as recruit proteins that bind to this curvature.
source: In cells, membrane curvature can both be induced by proteins that bind to membranes as well as recruit proteins that bind to this curvature (Peter et al., 2004; Renner and Weibel, 2011; Wang and Wingreen, 2013; Ursell et al., 2014; Hussain et al., 2018; Wu et al., 2018).
evidence: This claim is supported by multiple citations to prior work.

claim: MreB filaments polymerize onto membranes.
source: MreB filaments polymerize onto membranes (Figure 1A) (Salje et al., 2011; van den Ent et al., 2014; Hussain et al., 2018)
evidence: This claim is supported by citations and reference to Figure 1A showing cryo-EM images.

claim: MreB filaments create short filaments that move along their lengths in live cells.
source: MreB filaments polymerize onto membranes (Figure 1A) (Salje et al., 2011; van den Ent et al., 2014; Hussain et al., 2018), creating short filaments that move along their lengths in live cells.
evidence: This is stated as established knowledge about MreB behavior in cells.

claim: MreB filaments rotate around the rod width, a motion powered by the activity of associated cell wall synthesis enzymes.
source: Viewed dynamically, MreB filaments are seen to rotate around the rod width, a motion powered by the activity of associated cell wall synthesis enzymes (Figure 1B and Figure 1—video 1) (Garner et al., 2011; Domínguez-Escobar et al., 2011; van Teeffelen et al., 2011; Reimold et al., 2013; Hussain et al., 2018).
evidence: This claim is supported by multiple citations and reference to Figure 1B.

claim: The orientation of MreB filaments coincides with the direction of their motion, as filaments move along the direction in which they point.
source: The orientation of MreB filaments coincides with the direction of their motion, as filaments move along the direction in which they point (Figure 1C) (Hussain et al., 2018; Olshausen et al., 2013).
evidence: This claim is supported by citations and reference to Figure 1C showing angular distributions.

claim: In Escherichia coli, MreB filaments are enriched at regions of negative Gaussian curvature or small mean curvature.
source: However, studies examining the localization of MreB in kymographs (Ursell et al., 2014) or at single time points (Bratton et al., 2018) have found that, in Escherichia coli, MreB filaments are enriched at regions of negative Gaussian curvature or small mean curvature (Figure 1D).
evidence: This claim is supported by citations to prior experimental work and reference to Figure 1D.

claim: A typical filament (~250 nm long) in Bacillus subtilis moves through a 1 µm2 region in ~30 s.
source: As filaments are constantly moving, their instantaneous localization to any one point is transient: a typical filament (~250 nm long) in Bacillus subtilis moves through a 1 µm2 region in ~30 s.
evidence: This is a quantitative observation about MreB filament dynamics.

claim: MreB filaments orient and translocate along directions of largest principal curvature inside differently shaped B. subtilis cells and liposomes.
source: In previous work (Hussain et al., 2018), we demonstrated that MreB filaments orient and translocate along directions of largest principal curvature inside differently shaped B. subtilis cells and liposomes.
evidence: This claim is supported by citation to prior work by the authors.

claim: The dynamics of MreB translocation alone, without requiring any intrinsic preference of MreB filaments for curved regions of the cell, results in differential enrichment of MreB filaments at regions of negative Gaussian curvature or small mean curvature similar to those observed in cells.
source: Strikingly, we find that the dynamics of MreB translocation alone, without requiring any intrinsic preference of MreB filaments for curved regions of the cell, results in differential enrichment of MreB filaments at regions of negative Gaussian curvature or small mean curvature similar to those observed in cells.
evidence: This is a primary finding from the modeling work presented in the manuscript.

claim: Three different cryo-electron microscopy studies have shown that membrane-bound MreB filaments are flat and untwisted, binding to the membrane on one filament face.
source: While it is intriguing to examine the effects of filament rigidity and twist on general filament systems (discussed below), here we focus on modeling thin, inwardly curved MreB filaments with no twist. We focus on these parameters as they reflect the observations of all available in vitro studies of membrane-associated MreB: three different cryo-electron microscopy studies have shown that membrane-bound MreB filaments are flat and untwisted, binding to the membrane on one filament face (Figure 1A) (Salje et al., 2011; van den Ent et al., 2014; Hussain et al., 2018).
evidence: This claim is supported by citations to three cryo-EM studies and reference to Figure 1A.

claim: Inward curvature, and not twist, limits filament length for MreB.
source: These studies also suggest that inward curvature, and not twist, limits filament length: MreB filaments are short when polymerized onto non-deforming planar-supported lipid bilayers, but become extremely long when polymerized inside deformable liposomes (Salje et al., 2011; van den Ent et al., 2014; Hussain et al., 2018).
evidence: This claim is inferred from observations in cited studies about filament length in different contexts.

claim: Thin, untwisted filaments orient robustly along directions of largest principal curvature.
source: The model we present here extends our previous work (Hussain et al., 2018) and demonstrates that thin, untwisted filaments orient robustly along directions of largest principal curvature, thus providing a generic mechanism for orienting their motion.
evidence: This is a primary finding from the modeling work presented in the manuscript.

claim: The model predicts a preferred, circumferential orientation of MreB binding in a rod-shaped cell for characteristic parameter values relevant to the binding of MreB filaments to bacterial membranes.
source: For characteristic parameter values relevant to the binding of MreB filaments to bacterial membranes, as summarized in Supplementary file 1, our model predicts a preferred, circumferential orientation of MreB binding in a rod-shaped cell.
evidence: This is a prediction from the model presented in the manuscript.

claim: The preferred binding orientation arises because the intrinsic curvature of filaments is smaller than characteristic cell radii.
source: This result arises because the intrinsic curvature of filaments is smaller than characteristic cell radii.
evidence: This is an explanation for the model prediction based on the parameters used.

claim: Inside cells, MreB filaments move along the membrane in the direction of their orientation.
source: Inside cells, MreB filaments move along the membrane in the direction of their orientation (Hussain et al., 2018; Olshausen et al., 2013) (Figure 1C).
evidence: This claim is supported by citations and reference to Figure 1C.

claim: The directional and processive motion of MreB is driven by cell wall synthesis.
source: This directional and processive motion is driven by cell wall synthesis (Sliusarenko et al., 2010; van Teeffelen et al., 2011; Olshausen et al., 2013)
evidence: This claim is supported by citations to prior work.

claim: MreB filaments may reorient according to different membrane geometries.
source: This directional and processive motion is driven by cell wall synthesis (Sliusarenko et al., 2010; van Teeffelen et al., 2011; Olshausen et al., 2013), and filaments may reorient according to different membrane geometries (Hussain et al., 2018).
evidence: This claim is supported by citation to prior work.

claim: Highly-bent MreB filaments translocate along the direction of largest curvature, a direction that minimizes the energetic cost of binding.
source: Thus, highly-bent MreB filaments translocate along the direction of largest curvature, a direction that minimizes the energetic cost of binding.
evidence: This is a hypothesis based on the model and prior observations.

claim: MreB moves circumferentially in live B. subtilis cells, but this motion becomes disoriented if cells become round.
source: As discussed below, this hypothesis is supported by observations that (1) MreB moves circumferentially in live B. subtilis cells, but this motion becomes disoriented if cells become round
evidence: This is stated as an observation supporting the hypothesis, from prior work.

claim: Circumferential motion of MreB is re-established when round cells are confined into rods.
source: (2) circumferential motion is re-established when round cells are confined into rods
evidence: This is stated as an observation supporting the hypothesis, from prior work.

claim: MreB moves directionally in bulges protruding from round cells.
source: (3) MreB moves directionally in bulges protruding from round cells
evidence: This is stated as an observation supporting the hypothesis, from prior work.

claim: MreB filaments rapidly translocate out of poles in rods, reorienting when filaments reach the cylindrical bulks.
source: (4) MreB filaments rapidly translocate out of poles in rods, reorienting when filaments reach the cylindrical bulks (Hussain et al., 2018).
evidence: This is stated as an observation supporting the hypothesis, from cited prior work.

claim: The persistence time of MreB filaments in E. coli has been estimated as ~5 min.
source: Similar experiments have estimated the persistence time of MreB filaments in E. coli as ~5 min (Ursell et al., 2014)
evidence: This claim is supported by citation to prior experimental work.

claim: The distribution of MreB filament angles gradually becomes broader as B. subtilis cells become wider.
source: Furthermore, in recent studies, rod-shaped cells have been perturbed to be in geometries other than a spherocylinder (Ursell et al., 2014; Wong et al., 2017; Hussain et al., 2018; Renner et al., 2013; Amir et al., 2014). As the distribution of MreB filament angles gradually becomes broader as B. subtilis cells become wider (Hussain et al., 2018)
evidence: This claim is supported by citation to prior experimental work.

claim: The standard deviation of approximately 0.2 µm for the axial displacement of a filament per hoop of wall material inserted is consistent with experimental measurements.
source: This value is consistent with experimental measurements (Figure 3B), showing that deviations from a circumferential translocation direction can significantly contribute to wall insertions in the axial direction and disordered wall architecture.
evidence: This claim compares model predictions with experimental data shown in Figure 3B.

claim: MreB filaments have been observed to be depleted from the hemispherical poles of spherocylindrical cells compared to the cylindrical bulks.
source: MreB filaments have been observed to be depleted from the hemispherical poles of spherocylindrical cells compared to the cylindrical bulks (Kawazura et al., 2017; Ursell et al., 2014).
evidence: This claim is supported by citations to prior experimental work.

claim: MreB filaments reorient rapidly in, and translocate out of, the poles and into the bulks, where motion then becomes aligned.
source: Observations of filament dynamics revealed a possible explanation: MreB filaments reorient rapidly in, and translocate out of, the poles and into the bulks, where motion then becomes aligned (Hussain et al., 2018).
evidence: This claim is supported by citation to prior experimental work.

claim: Simulations of Equation (3) on a spherocylindrical surface show that the concentration of filaments in the bulk is enhanced.
source: Consistent with this observation, simulations of Equation (3) on a spherocylindrical surface show that the concentration of filaments in the bulk is enhanced (Figure 3C).
evidence: This is a finding from simulations presented in the manuscript, shown in Figure 3C.

claim: The average filament concentration is predicted to be approximately two-fold higher in the bulk than the poles.
source: The average filament concentration is predicted to be approximately two-fold higher in the bulk than the poles, in agreement with experimental measurements in E. coli (Ursell et al., 2014).
evidence: This is a prediction from the model that agrees with cited experimental measurements.

claim: Simulations of Equation (3) on a toroidal surface are quantitatively consistent with prior measurements of MreB fluorescence in E. coli cells confined to donut-shaped microchambers.
source: Simulations of Equation (3) on a toroidal surface are also quantitatively consistent with prior measurements of MreB fluorescence in E. coli cells confined to donut-shaped microchambers, which have shown that MreB intensity is increased at the inner edges by a factor of ∼1.1 relative to the midlines (Figure 3D) (Wong et al., 2017).
evidence: This claim compares model predictions with experimental data from cited work, shown in Figure 3D.

claim: For a spherocylinder, filament enrichment arises because the cylindrical bulk retains filaments: oriented motion is preserved in the bulk, while disordered motion at the poles eventually becomes ordered.
source: For a spherocylinder, filament enrichment arises because the cylindrical bulk retains filaments: oriented motion is preserved in the bulk, while disordered motion at the poles eventually becomes ordered.
evidence: This is an explanation for the mechanism of enrichment based on the model.

claim: In a curved cell, filament enrichment arises because filaments become uniformly distributed along circumferential hoops, and the smaller arclength along the inner edge results in a greater density of filaments.
source: In contrast, filament enrichment arises in a curved cell because filaments become uniformly distributed along circumferential hoops. The smaller arclength along the inner edge then results in a greater density of filaments.
evidence: This is an explanation for the mechanism of enrichment based on the model.

claim: MreB rotation and localization at small protrusions in B. subtilis protoplasts preceded rod shape generation from these protrusions.
source: In our previous study, we found that MreB rotation and localization at small protrusions in B. subtilis protoplasts preceded rod shape generation from these protrusions (Hussain et al., 2018).
evidence: This claim is supported by citation to prior work by the authors.

claim: Simulations of Equation (3) on a cylindrical body with a protruding bulge reveal that the filament concentration is larger in the bulge.
source: Simulations of Equation (3) on this geometry reveal that the filament concentration is larger in the bulge and that the predicted enrichment is quantitatively consistent with the MreB enhancement observed in bulged cells, without any fitting parameters (Figure 3E and Figure 3—figure supplement 1).
evidence: This is a finding from simulations presented in the manuscript, shown in Figure 3E.

claim: The predicted enrichment in bulges is quantitatively consistent with the MreB enhancement observed in bulged cells, without any fitting parameters.
source: Simulations of Equation (3) on this geometry reveal that the filament concentration is larger in the bulge and that the predicted enrichment is quantitatively consistent with the MreB enhancement observed in bulged cells, without any fitting parameters (Figure 3E and Figure 3—figure supplement 1).
evidence: This claim compares model predictions with experimental observations, shown in Figure 3E.

claim: For a bulged cylinder, localization arises due to the bulge attracting filaments.
source: Similar to the case of a spherocylinder, localization arises due to the bulge attracting filaments.
evidence: This is an explanation for the mechanism of enrichment based on the model.

claim: The dynamics of Equation (3) results in localization which contributes to de novo generation of rod shape.
source: The dynamics of Equation (3) therefore results in localization which contributes to de novo generation of rod shape.
evidence: This is a conclusion drawn from the model results.

claim: The empirically observed magnitudes of MreB enrichment at regions of negative Gaussian curvature or small mean curvature in E. coli cells with submicron-scale shape fluctuations or confined in sinusoidal chambers are consistent with the modeling.
source: Finally, previous work has examined MreB localization in E. coli cells (1) with submicron-scale shape fluctuations or (2) confined in sinusoidal chambers (Ursell et al., 2014; Shi et al., 2017; Bratton et al., 2018). The empirically observed magnitudes of MreB enrichment at regions of negative Gaussian curvature or small mean curvature in these studies are consistent with our modeling.
evidence: This claim compares model predictions with experimental observations from cited studies.

claim: The Gaussian and mean curvatures in the undulating geometry are positively correlated and consistent with experimental observations.
source: As discussed in Appendix 1, the Gaussian and mean curvatures in this geometry are positively correlated and consistent with experimental observations (Ursell et al., 2014).
evidence: This is a finding from the model that is consistent with cited experimental observations.

claim: The enrichment at regions of negative Gaussian curvature or small mean curvature arises because the principal curvatures away from these regions reorient filaments axially, instead of circumferentially, so that regions of negative Gaussian curvature or small mean curvature attract filaments.
source: This effect arises because the principal curvatures away from these regions reorient filaments axially, instead of circumferentially, so that regions of negative Gaussian curvature or small mean curvature attract filaments.
evidence: This is an explanation for the mechanism of enrichment based on the model.

claim: The magnitude of enhancement at regions of negative Gaussian curvature or small mean curvature is consistent with the amount of MreB enrichment observed.
source: Furthermore, the magnitude of this enhancement is consistent with the amount of MreB enrichment observed (Figure 3G and Figure 3—figure supplement 3), demonstrating that translocation dynamics alone can negatively correlate filament concentration with Gaussian or mean curvature in cells with similar short wavelength undulations.
evidence: This claim compares model predictions with experimental observations, shown in Figure 3G.

claim: Translocation dynamics alone can negatively correlate filament concentration with Gaussian or mean curvature in cells with similar short wavelength undulations.
source: Furthermore, the magnitude of this enhancement is consistent with the amount of MreB enrichment observed (Figure 3G and Figure 3—figure supplement 3), demonstrating that translocation dynamics alone can negatively correlate filament concentration with Gaussian or mean curvature in cells with similar short wavelength undulations.
evidence: This is a conclusion drawn from the model results.

claim: The magnitude of the localization can be quantitatively predicted by geometric parameters alone.
source: The magnitude of the localization can be quantitatively predicted by geometric parameters alone (Appendix 1).
evidence: This is a finding from the model presented in the manuscript.

claim: A nonzero processivity is required for localization even in geometries which attract filaments.
source: Nevertheless, a nonzero processivity is required for localization even in geometries which attract filaments (Figure 4B and Figure 4—figure supplements 1 and 2).
evidence: This is a finding from the model presented in the manuscript, shown in Figure 4B.

claim: Large filament bundles or twist have not been observed in MreB filaments reconstituted in vitro.
source: Finally, while large filament bundles or twist have not been observed in MreB filaments reconstituted in vitro (Salje et al., 2011; van den Ent et al., 2014; Hussain et al., 2018)
evidence: This claim is supported by citations to prior experimental work.

claim: General filament systems could exhibit large filament bundles or twist.
source: Finally, while large filament bundles or twist have not been observed in MreB filaments reconstituted in vitro (Salje et al., 2011; van den Ent et al., 2014; Hussain et al., 2018), it is possible that general filament systems could exhibit these properties (Wang and Wingreen, 2013; Quint et al., 2016).
evidence: This is speculation about other filament systems, supported by citations.

claim: The binding and activation of twisted filaments may depend on membrane Gaussian curvature.
source: The binding and activation of twisted filaments may also depend on membrane Gaussian curvature, as previously demonstrated (Quint et al., 2016).
evidence: This claim is supported by citation to prior work.

claim: Model predictions remain largely robust across a broad range of filament bending rigidity, filament twist, and Gaussian curvature-dependent activation parameters.
source: We systematically explore the effects of varying filament bending rigidity, filament twist, and Gaussian curvature-dependent activation in Appendix 1, where we show that our model predictions remain largely robust across a broad range of these parameters (Figure 4—figure supplement 4).
evidence: This is a finding from the model presented in the manuscript, shown in Figure 4—figure supplement 4.

claim: Filament dynamics are expected to contribute to localization in different filament systems, regardless of the details of filament rigidity, twist, and other parameters of the model.
source: Thus, we expect filament dynamics to contribute to localization in different filament systems, regardless of the details of filament rigidity, twist, and other parameters of our model.
evidence: This is a conclusion drawn from the robustness analysis of the model.

claim: The main contribution of this work is to show that the biological results of MreB localization, as observed in many different experiments involving a range of cell shapes, can arise from processivity and principal curvature-dependent motion alone.
source: The main contribution of this work is to show that the biological results of MreB localization, as observed in many different experiments involving a range of cell shapes (Hussain et al., 2018; Wong et al., 2017; Ursell et al., 2014; Shi et al., 2017; Bratton et al., 2018), can arise from processivity and principal curvature-dependent motion alone.
evidence: This is a summary statement of the main contribution of the work.

claim: The localization of translocating protein filaments can vary significantly depending on membrane geometry.
source: More broadly, our work shows that the localization of translocating protein filaments can vary significantly depending on membrane geometry.
evidence: This is a general conclusion drawn from the work.

claim: In bacterial cytokinesis, filaments of the tubulin homolog FtsZ assemble at, and treadmill around, the septum, a process which directs the insertion of new PG and constricts the cell.
source: For example, in bacterial cytokinesis, filaments of the tubulin homolog FtsZ assemble at, and treadmill around, the septum, a process which directs the insertion of new PG and constricts the cell (Bisson-Filho et al., 2017; Yang et al., 2017).
evidence: This claim is supported by citations to prior work.

claim: Like MreB, FtsZ filaments are curved and could orient along the largest principal direction on membranes through bending alone.
source: Like MreB, FtsZ filaments are curved and could orient along the largest principal direction on membranes through bending alone (Osawa et al., 2009; Erickson et al., 2010).
evidence: This is speculation about FtsZ behavior based on similarity to MreB, supported by citations.

claim: Treadmilling of FtsZ along the largest principal direction would allow filaments to drive PG synthesis circumferentially at the septum.
source: Treadmilling along such directions would then allow filaments to drive PG synthesis circumferentially at the septum.
evidence: This is speculation about FtsZ function based on the model.

claim: Septins, BAR-domain-containing proteins, dynamins, and endoproteins are known to exhibit curvature-dependent membrane binding behaviors important for membrane trafficking, growth, and movement in both prokaryotes and eukaryotes.
source: Aside from MreB and FtsZ, septins, BAR-domain-containing proteins, dynamins, and endoproteins are known to exhibit similar, curvature-dependent membrane binding behaviors important for membrane trafficking, growth, and movement in both prokaryotes and eukaryotes (Baumgart et al., 2011; Zimmerberg and Kozlov, 2006; McMahon and Gallop, 2005; Peter et al., 2004; Low and Löwe, 2006; Raiborg and Stenmark, 2009; Teo et al., 2006; Kostelansky et al., 2007).
evidence: This claim is supported by multiple citations to prior work.

claim: Like MreB filaments, many proteins that exhibit curvature-dependent membrane binding sense membrane curvature through mechanical deformations of either the membrane or the protein itself.
source: Like MreB filaments, many such proteins sense membrane curvature through mechanical deformations of either the membrane or the protein itself.
evidence: This is stated as general knowledge about curvature-sensing proteins.

claim: BAR-domain-containing proteins scaffold higher-order assemblies of dynamin that actively constrict for vesicle scission.
source: One example is BAR-domain-containing proteins, which scaffold higher-order assemblies of dynamin that actively constrict for vesicle scission (McMahon and Gallop, 2005).
evidence: This claim is supported by citation to prior work.

claim: Systems where molecules bind to membranes or sense membrane curvature are widespread and involved in pathogenesis, cell division, intracellular trafficking, and cell migration.
source: These systems are widespread and involved in pathogenesis (Baumgart et al., 2011; Frost et al., 2009), cell division (Renner et al., 2013; Ramamurthi and Losick, 2009; Ramamurthi et al., 2009; Frost et al., 2009), intracellular trafficking (Zimmerberg and Kozlov, 2006; McMahon and Gallop, 2005; Raiborg and Stenmark, 2009; Ford et al., 2002; Frost et al., 2009; Römer et al., 2007), and cell migration (Frost et al., 2009; Zhao et al., 2013).
evidence: This claim is supported by multiple citations to prior work.

claim: The mathematical model introduced in this work requires minimal assumptions as to how filaments bind to and translocate on membranes.
source: The mathematical model introduced in this work, which requires minimal assumptions as to how filaments bind to and translocate on membranes, should be widely applicable to these and other broader contexts.
evidence: This is a statement about the generality of the model.

claim: The mathematical model should be widely applicable to systems involving membrane curvature sensing and protein localization.
source: The mathematical model introduced in this work, which requires minimal assumptions as to how filaments bind to and translocate on membranes, should be widely applicable to these and other broader contexts.
evidence: This is speculation about the applicability of the model to other systems.

claim: MreB filaments directly bind to membranes as shown by cryo-electron microscopy.
source: Cryo-electron microscopy image showing the direct membrane binding of MreB filaments reconstituted in vitro to vesicles.
evidence: This is shown in Figure 1A with citation to the source study.

claim: MreB filaments translocate in live Bacillus subtilis cells with trajectories perpendicular to the cellular long axis.
source: Fluorescence microscopy image of MreB filaments translocating in live Bacillus subtilis cells with trajectories of individual filaments drawn and cell edges outlined, reproduced from Hussain et al. (2018) (see also Figure 1—video 1). Note that typical trajectories are perpendicular to the cellular long axis, consistent with the binding angles in (C).
evidence: This is shown in Figure 1B with citation to the source study.

claim: The angular distribution of membrane-bound filaments within B. subtilis protoplasts confined to become rod-shaped is similar to MreB motion in wild-type B. subtilis cells.
source: Angular distribution of membrane-bound filaments within B. subtilis protoplasts confined to become rod-shaped (green curve) and MreB motion in wild-type B. subtilis cells (black curve), reproduced from Hussain et al. (2018).
evidence: This is shown in Figure 1C where the two curves overlap substantially.

claim: Negative/positive Gaussian curvature correlates with more/less MreB in E. coli cells growing in a sinusoidally shaped chamber.
source: Relative MreB enrichment in Escherichia coli cells growing in a sinusoidally shaped chamber, adapted from Ursell et al. (2014).
evidence: This is shown in Figure 1D with citation to the source study.
